The poem describes a huge casuarina tree in her family garden at Baugmaree, entwined by a creeper 'like a python', where a grey baboon sits at dawn, birds sing and cows graze beneath.

The tree is dear to her because she and her beloved brother and sister (Abju and Aru, who both died young) played under it. Its sound, which she seems to hear even in France and Italy, becomes a 'dirge-like murmur' of mourning. She hopes to consecrate the tree to memory, as Wordsworth's yew trees of Borrowdale were, and wishes it may be 'Unknown, yet well-known to the eye of faith' - remembered through her poem. Romantic influence (Wordsworth, Keats) blends with Indian scenery.

sections.title: In the Zoo – A. K. Ramanujan

blocks.text: A prescribed poem by Ramanujan. Students should study its imagery, observation, voice and treatment of the human relationship with the zoo and its inhabitants from the assigned text.

A. K. Ramanujan (1929-1993) was a poet, translator and scholar of Kannada and Tamil literature who taught at the University of Chicago. His poetry is known for precise observation, irony, unexpected images and a cool, detached tone, often exploring family, memory, the body and the gap between Indian and Western experience.

When studying this poem, note how the speaker observes the animals in captivity, what details are selected, how the poem might compare animals and people (for example, enclosed, watched, tamed or displaced) and the tone - ironic, sympathetic or detached. Ramanujan's poems often end with a surprising turn that changes the meaning of what came before, so pay close attention to the last lines of the prescribed text.
The poem creates an image of absence and searching. Its compact imagery invites reflection on identity, loss and the difficulty of locating the self.

Jayanta Mahapatra (1928-2023) was an Odia physicist who started writing poetry in his forties and became one of the leading Indian English poets; he received the Sahitya Akademi Award for 'Relationship' (1981). His poetry is known for silence, mood and images of Odisha - Puri, temples, rain, poverty and women.

'A Missing Person' is a very short poem. A woman in a darkened room tries to find herself in a mirror, but cannot see her reflection, while the dark shadows of the room absorb her. The imagery suggests a woman whose identity has been erased, perhaps by her life, her role or loneliness - she is 'missing' while still present. The compression of the poem forces the reader to fill the gaps, which is typical of Mahapatra.

The poem describes a collective journey that begins with enthusiasm but gradually loses unity and purpose. It can be read as a reflection on idealism, conflict, disappointment and the meaning of pilgrimage.

Nissim Ezekiel (1924-2004), a Bombay poet of the Bene Israel Jewish community, is often called the father of modern Indian English poetry. 'Enterprise' appears in 'The Unfinished Man' (1960). A group sets out on a journey 'to see an ancient city', at first full of confidence and purpose ('It started as a pilgrimage, / Exalting minds and making all / The burdens light').

Gradually the group meets difficulties - heat, quarrels about how to write a statement, an attack by local people, members leaving - until 'when we reached the place, / We hardly knew why we had come'. The poem ends: 'Home is where we have to gather grace.' The journey can be read as any ambitious human enterprise (spiritual, political or artistic) that loses its meaning through conflict and pride. The conclusion suggests that grace is found in ordinary daily life, not in grand pursuits.

The play presents a disturbing future in which poverty and global inequality turn the human body into a commodity. It explores exploitation, technology, consumer power and the unequal relationship between rich and poor societies.

Manjula Padmanabhan's 'Harvest' won the Onassis Prize for theatre in 1997. Set in Bombay in a near future, it shows Om Prakash, an unemployed young man, who signs a contract with InterPlanta Services to sell his organs to a rich foreign 'receiver'. In return his family gets money, luxury goods and modern appliances. A Contact Module is installed in their one-room home, through which the glamorous Ginni, apparently a young American woman, watches and controls them.

The family includes Om's wife Jaya, his mother Ma, and his younger brother Jeetu, who is taken by mistake. Ma becomes addicted to a 'super-deluxe video coach'. At the end it is revealed that 'Ginni' is a computer image hiding Virgil, an old man who wants a young body. Jaya refuses to give him what he wants and threatens to kill herself, asserting control over her own body. The play criticises organ trade, globalisation, surveillance and the commodification of poor bodies by rich nations.
Balram Halwai narrates his rise from poverty and servitude to entrepreneurship. The novel examines class inequality, corruption, ambition, violence and the darker side of economic change in India.

Aravind Adiga's debut novel won the Man Booker Prize in 2008. It is written as a series of letters over seven nights from Balram Halwai, a Bangalore entrepreneur, to the Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao, who is about to visit India. Balram was born in Laxmangarh in the 'Darkness' (the poor rural India of the Ganges plain), worked in a tea shop and became a driver for the son of a rich landlord, Ashok, and his wife Pinky Madam, in Delhi.

He explains the 'Rooster Coop' - the system that keeps the poor servants loyal to their masters as roosters wait in a cage to be slaughtered. After seeing corruption, bribery and how Pinky Madam's hit-and-run accident is blamed on him, Balram murders Ashok, steals a bag of money and escapes to Bangalore, where he starts a taxi business for call centres. He calls himself 'the White Tiger', a rare creature who escapes the coop. The novel uses dark humour and an unreliable narrator.

sections.title: Indian Writing in English: Background and Poetry

blocks.text:
The course introduces Indian Writing in English through A. K. Mehrotra and then moves across poetry, drama and fiction. The poetry unit includes Toru Dutt, A. K. Ramanujan, Jayanta Mahapatra and Nissim Ezekiel.

Our Casuarina Tree links nature with memory and loss. A Missing Person uses compressed imagery around absence and identity. Enterprise turns a journey into a reflection on idealism and disappointment. For Ramanujan's In the Zoo, students should base detailed interpretation on the prescribed poem.

Phases of Indian English poetry: (1) pioneers of the nineteenth century, such as Derozio, Toru Dutt and Manmohan Ghose, who wrote in Romantic and Victorian styles; (2) Sri Aurobindo, Sarojini Naidu and Tagore (in English translation), who expressed spiritual and nationalist themes; (3) modern poets after 1947 - Ezekiel, Ramanujan, Mahapatra, Kamala Das, R. Parthasarathy, Gieve Patel - who used everyday language, irony and personal experience and asked how to write Indian poetry in English.

Toru Dutt's 'Our Casuarina Tree' is Romantic: the tree is a symbol of permanence, memory and love for her dead siblings, and the poem aims to immortalise it. Ramanujan's 'In the Zoo' shows his characteristic precise observation and irony. Mahapatra's 'A Missing Person' uses minimal language and dark imagery to express the loss of identity, possibly of a woman. Ezekiel's 'Enterprise' presents an allegory of a failed journey and concludes with the importance of the ordinary home.

In an answer, comment on how these poets use English: Toru Dutt follows English models but uses Indian scenery; the modern poets develop an Indian voice through irony, local detail and colloquial rhythms. Their themes include memory, identity, the family, disillusionment and the relationship between the individual and society.

Manjula Padmanabhan's Harvest imagines a world in which economically vulnerable people can be drawn into arrangements where their bodies become resources for wealthy outsiders.

The play uses technology and a futuristic situation to examine poverty, exploitation, global inequality and commodification. It asks what happens to dignity and autonomy when survival itself is controlled by economic power.

Harvest is a dystopian play. The futuristic setting (around 2010 from a 1990s perspective) exaggerates trends that already existed: international organ trading, the outsourcing of labour, the spread of television and consumer goods, and surveillance technology. The Contact Module, through which Ginni speaks and watches, symbolises how global capital and media enter and control the homes of the poor.

Characters: Om Prakash sells his body because he has lost his job and sees no other way; his choice is presented as voluntary but driven by poverty. Ma is seduced by consumer goods and finally shuts herself in a video coach, a symbol of escape into entertainment. Jeetu, a sex worker, is more rebellious but is also consumed. Jaya, the most independent character, resists and finally refuses Virgil's demands, insisting that her body is hers and she would rather die than be used.

Themes and interpretation: the play is a critique of neo-colonialism, in which rich First World countries exploit the bodies and resources of the Third World; the commodification of the human body; the breakdown of family relationships under economic pressure; gender, especially Jaya's struggle for control over her body; and the dehumanising effects of technology. Padmanabhan uses dark comedy and irony, and the ending suggests that resistance is possible even in a world dominated by global markets.

Aravind Adiga's The White Tiger is narrated by Balram Halwai, who describes his movement from poverty and servitude toward wealth and independence. His story exposes deep inequality between privileged and poor India.

Balram's success is morally complicated, making the novel more than a simple success story. Corruption, class, violence, ambition and economic transformation are central themes. The first-person narrative also forces readers to confront the narrator's own justification of his actions.

Narrative technique: the novel is an epistolary first-person narrative addressed to Wen Jiabao. This allows Balram to compare India with China, to mock official images of India as a modern democracy and to speak with sarcasm and humour. Because he is justifying a murder, he is an unreliable narrator, and readers must judge his account.

Themes: (1) inequality between 'India of Light' and 'India of Darkness', and between masters and servants; (2) corruption - in politics, elections (Balram's vote is sold), police and business; (3) the 'Rooster Coop' and the family as instruments that keep the poor in servitude - Balram's escape costs the lives of his relatives, whom the landlord's family likely kills in revenge; (4) entrepreneurship and globalisation - Bangalore's outsourcing boom represents the new India, but success is built on crime and bribery; (5) identity and freedom - Balram rejects his given name 'Munna' and becomes Ashok Sharma, a self-made man.

Critical views: some praised the novel for exposing the dark side of India's economic growth; others criticised it as presenting India through Western stereotypes. In an answer, discuss how Adiga uses satire and dark humour, the symbolism of the white tiger and the rooster coop, and the moral ambiguity of Balram's success.
Androcentrism places male experience or perspective at the centre and treats it as the general norm.

The term was popularised by the American sociologist Charlotte Perkins Gilman in 'The Man-Made World; or, Our Androcentric Culture' (1911). In literature and culture, androcentrism appears when men are assumed to be the normal subject (the generic 'he' or 'mankind'), when history or literature is written mainly about men, and when women are defined only in relation to men - as wives, mothers or daughters.

Simone de Beauvoir described the same idea: man is the Subject, woman the Other. Feminist criticism exposes androcentric assumptions in the literary canon and in critical judgements, and recovers neglected women writers.
Androgyny refers to the combination or crossing of characteristics conventionally labelled masculine and feminine.

In literary theory, androgyny is especially associated with Virginia Woolf's 'A Room of One's Own' (1929). Following Coleridge's remark that 'a great mind is androgynous', Woolf argued that the best creative mind combines masculine and feminine qualities, and that it is 'fatal to be a man or woman pure and simple'. Her novel 'Orlando' (1928) presents a hero who changes sex over centuries.

Later feminists debated the idea: some saw androgyny as freeing people from rigid gender roles, while others feared it erased women's specific experiences. Today it is related to discussions of gender fluidity and non-binary identities.
Confessional writing uses personal experiences, emotions and private struggles as important literary material.

The term 'confessional poetry' was used by critic M. L. Rosenthal in 1959 about Robert Lowell's 'Life Studies'. Confessional poets - Lowell, Sylvia Plath, Anne Sexton, W. D. Snodgrass and, in India, Kamala Das - wrote openly about mental illness, suicide attempts, sexuality, divorce, family conflict and the body, topics previously considered too private for poetry.

For women writers, confession was a way to break silence about experiences such as domestic oppression, motherhood and desire. The first-person speaker seems autobiographical, but critics warn that the 'I' is still a constructed persona, so the poem should not be read simply as a diary.
Feminism challenges gender inequality. The syllabus introduces first, second and third waves to show changing priorities and forms of feminist thought and activism.

First-wave feminism (late nineteenth to early twentieth century) fought for legal rights, especially women's suffrage, property and education rights; key texts include Mary Wollstonecraft's 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman' (1792). Second-wave feminism (1960s-1980s) addressed sexuality, family, work, reproductive rights and cultural representation, with the slogan 'the personal is political'; key texts are Simone de Beauvoir's 'The Second Sex' (1949), Betty Friedan's 'The Feminine Mystique' (1963) and Kate Millett's 'Sexual Politics' (1970).

Third-wave feminism (1990s onward) emphasised diversity and intersectionality (a term coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989) - recognising that race, class, sexuality and nationality shape women's experiences differently - and challenged universal definitions of 'woman'. The plural 'feminisms' recognises that there are many kinds, such as liberal, radical, Marxist/socialist, black, postcolonial and ecofeminism. A fourth wave using social media (for example, #MeToo) is sometimes identified.
Patriarchy is a social system in which men hold dominant power and authority in major institutions and relationships.

Literally 'rule of the father', patriarchy describes a social system in which men hold primary power in the family, politics, religion, economy and culture, and in which women are subordinated. Kate Millett's 'Sexual Politics' (1970) argued that patriarchy is the most pervasive ideology of our culture, maintained through socialisation, family, religion, law and literature.

Feminist critics show how literature can reinforce patriarchy (by idealising passive women or punishing independent ones) or challenge it. Sylvia Walby identified six structures of patriarchy: household production, paid work, the state, male violence, sexuality and cultural institutions. Patriarchy also harms men by imposing rigid expectations of masculinity.
Gender refers to socially shaped roles and expectations associated with sex categories. Masculinities studies the different social forms through which manhood is constructed.

Feminists distinguish between sex (biological categories) and gender (culturally constructed roles). De Beauvoir's statement 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' expresses this. Judith Butler ('Gender Trouble', 1990) went further, arguing that gender is performative - produced by repeated acts and behaviour rather than expressing a fixed inner essence.

Masculinity studies, associated with R. W. Connell, examines how ideas of manhood are constructed. Connell's concept of 'hegemonic masculinity' describes the dominant form (strong, aggressive, emotionally restrained, heterosexual) that is valued above subordinate masculinities and femininity. Literature such as Macbeth (where courage is tied to violence) and Things Fall Apart (Okonkwo's fear of appearing weak) can be read through this lens.
'The Other' describes people defined as different from a dominant norm. 'Subaltern' refers broadly to socially or politically marginalised groups with limited access to dominant power.

The 'Other' comes from philosophy (Hegel) and was used by Simone de Beauvoir: man defines himself as the Subject, the Absolute, and woman is defined as the Other in relation to him. Edward Said ('Orientalism', 1978) showed how the West constructed the 'Orient' as its Other. Othering means treating a group as fundamentally different and inferior.

The term 'subaltern' comes from Antonio Gramsci, who used it for groups excluded from dominant power structures. Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak's essay 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988) argued that the subaltern woman, especially in colonial India, is doubly silenced - by colonialism and patriarchy - and cannot easily be heard in dominant discourses. Spivak also translated Mahasweta Devi's 'Draupadi'.
Gender stereotypes are fixed and simplified beliefs about how women and men are expected to behave.

Examples include beliefs that women are emotional, weak, nurturing and suited to domestic work, while men are rational, strong, ambitious and suited to leadership; that girls are bad at mathematics; or that men should not cry. Stereotypes are learned through family, schools, media, advertising, religion and literature.

Stereotypes are harmful because they limit people's choices, justify discrimination and make those who do not conform feel abnormal. Feminist criticism identifies stereotypical images of women in literature, such as the 'angel in the house', the temptress or the madwoman, and shows how women writers rewrite them, as Carol Ann Duffy does with the passive heroine of Little Red Riding Hood.
The mirror speaks as an apparently exact observer while a woman confronts ageing and changing identity. The poem explores self-image, truth, time and anxiety about appearance.

Sylvia Plath (1932-1963), an American poet associated with confessional poetry, wrote 'Mirror' in 1961. It has two stanzas of nine lines. In the first, the mirror speaks: 'I am silver and exact. I have no preconceptions.' It claims to be 'not cruel, only truthful', 'the eye of a little god', and spends most of its time looking at the pink speckled wall opposite.

In the second stanza the mirror becomes a lake, and a woman bends over it 'Searching my reaches for what she really is'. She turns to 'those liars, the candles or the moon', but returns. The poem ends: 'In me she has drowned a young girl, and in me an old woman / Rises toward her day after day, like a terrible fish.' The poem explores ageing, women's anxiety about appearance in a society that values youthful beauty, and the search for true identity.

sections.title: I'm Wife; I've Finished That – Emily Dickinson

blocks.text: Dickinson's poem examines the change in female identity associated with marriage. Its language questions the categories through which a woman's social position is defined.

Emily Dickinson (1830-1886), the American poet who lived reclusively in Amherst, never married. The poem (numbered 199 by Johnson, around 1860) begins: 'I'm ‘wife’ - I've finished that - / That other state - / I'm Czar - I'm ‘Woman’ now - / It's safer so -'. The speaker compares girlhood to a painful earthly life seen from heaven ('This being comfort - then / That other kind - was pain'), and ends abruptly: 'I'm ‘Wife’! Stop there!'

The poem can be read ironically: marriage seems to give the woman a new title and status ('Czar', 'Woman') but may end her independent self, and the final command suggests she refuses to think further about what she has lost. Dickinson's dashes, capitals and compressed syntax make the poem ambiguous, allowing both a celebratory and a critical reading of marriage as a change in identity.

sections.title: Little Red Cap – Carol Ann Duffy

blocks.text: Duffy rewrites the Little Red Riding Hood story from a female perspective. The poem links sexuality, literary apprenticeship, power and the development of an independent poetic voice.

Carol Ann Duffy (born 1955) was Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom from 2009 to 2019, the first woman in that role. 'Little Red-Cap' opens her collection 'The World's Wife' (1999), in which famous stories are retold from women's viewpoints. The speaker, at the end of childhood, meets the wolf at the edge of town - he is reading poetry aloud - and goes with him into the woods, attracted by his books and words.

The wolf can be read as an older male poet (often linked to Ted Hughes); the girl gives up her virginity and learns from him, but after ten years she finds his poetry stale. She takes an axe to the wolf, finds her grandmother's bones in his belly, and walks out 'singing, all alone'. The poem rewrites the fairy tale: the girl is not rescued by a man but frees herself, symbolically breaking away from male literary tradition to find her own voice.

The play examines women, career, power and the costs of success within unequal social structures. Marlene's professional achievement is placed beside the experiences of women from different historical and social positions.

Caryl Churchill's 'Top Girls' (1982) was written during Margaret Thatcher's government. Act 1 is a dinner party held by Marlene, newly promoted managing director of the 'Top Girls' employment agency, attended by famous women from history and art: Isabella Bird (Victorian traveller), Lady Nijo (thirteenth-century Japanese courtesan turned nun), Dull Gret (from Brueghel's painting, who led women against devils in hell), Pope Joan (legendary female pope) and Patient Griselda (the obedient wife from Chaucer). They talk over each other, revealing what each sacrificed, especially their children.

Later scenes show Marlene at work and with her working-class sister Joyce, who has raised Marlene's daughter Angie, a girl with limited prospects. Marlene admires Thatcher; Joyce is socialist. The play uses overlapping dialogue, an all-female cast with doubling of roles and non-chronological structure. It asks whether women's success in a capitalist system that rewards competition is liberation, or merely the adoption of male values at the cost of other women.
The story centres on Dopdi Mejhen, an Adivasi woman subjected to state violence. Her final refusal to be shamed turns the violated body into an act of resistance.

Mahasweta Devi (1926-2016), Bengali writer and activist for tribal rights, wrote 'Draupadi' in 1978; Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak translated it in 1981. Dopdi Mejhen is a Santhal tribal woman who, with her husband Dulna, joined the Naxalite movement. They killed a landlord in a drought when upper-caste landlords denied water to tribals. Dulna is killed and Dopdi becomes a wanted rebel. Senanayak, an army officer who understands the rebels' theory, leads Operation Bakuli to capture her.

After she is captured, Senanayak orders his men to 'make her' (interrogate her) and she is raped repeatedly through the night. In the morning, she tears her cloth, refuses to cover herself and walks naked to Senanayak, saying: 'You can strip me, but how can you clothe me again? Are you a man?' and 'There isn't a man here that I should be ashamed.' Unlike the epic Draupadi, who is saved by Krishna, Dopdi has no divine protector; she turns her wounded body into a weapon of defiance that terrifies the officer.
The novel follows Celie's movement from abuse and silence toward independence, self-respect and supportive relationships. It explores race, gender, violence, sisterhood and empowerment.

Alice Walker's 'The Color Purple' (1982) won the Pulitzer Prize in 1983, the first by an African American woman for fiction. It is set in rural Georgia in the early twentieth century. Celie, a poor black girl, is repeatedly raped by the man she thinks is her father (Alphonso, actually her stepfather), who gives away her two children. She is married off to Mister (Albert), who beats her, and is separated from her beloved sister Nettie.

Written as letters to God and later to Nettie, the novel traces Celie's growth. Shug Avery, a blues singer and Mister's lover, becomes her friend and lover, teaching her self-love and a new idea of God. Sofia, who refuses to submit to men or white people, is imprisoned. Celie discovers that Mister hid Nettie's letters from Africa, where Nettie works as a missionary among the Olinka. Celie leaves Mister, starts a business making trousers, inherits her house and is finally reunited with Nettie and her children.

The syllabus introduces androcentrism, androgyny, confessional mode, feminisms, patriarchy, gender, masculinities, the Other, subalternity and gender stereotypes. These concepts provide tools for understanding how literature represents gender and power.

They help students ask who has authority, whose experience is treated as normal, how social roles are constructed and how marginalised voices resist dominant expectations.

These concepts come from feminist theory and gender studies. Androcentrism and patriarchy describe how society and culture put men at the centre and give them power. The Other (de Beauvoir) shows that woman is defined in relation to man. Gender as a social construction explains that roles such as wife and mother are learned, not natural, and masculinity studies shows that men's roles are also constructed. Stereotypes are the simplified images that maintain these roles.

Androgyny (Woolf) proposes a creative mind that combines masculine and feminine qualities. The confessional mode gives women writers a way to speak about private, previously taboo experiences. The idea of the subaltern (Spivak) reminds us that women are not one group: poor, tribal, colonised or black women face multiple layers of oppression, so the voices of Dopdi Mejhen and Celie must be heard alongside middle-class Western women.

The waves of feminism provide historical context: the first wave won legal rights, the second wave examined personal life and representation, and the third emphasised diversity and intersectionality. In an essay, define the main concepts briefly and apply them to the prescribed texts - e.g. patriarchy and stereotypes in Top Girls, the subaltern in Draupadi, confessional mode in Plath, and gender identity in Dickinson and Duffy.

Sylvia Plath's Mirror explores ageing, self-image and the desire for truthful reflection. Emily Dickinson's I'm Wife; I've Finished That examines the shift in social identity created by marriage.

Carol Ann Duffy's Little Red Cap rewrites a familiar tale to present female sexual and artistic development. Together, the poems demonstrate different ways women poets question identity, gender expectations and the construction of female experience.

Plath's 'Mirror' personifies the mirror and the lake. The mirror's claim to be objective ('I have no preconceptions') contrasts with the woman's emotional response - tears and agitation. The poem suggests that women are trained to measure their worth by appearance and youth, and the final image of the 'terrible fish' expresses fear of ageing. It also reflects Plath's concern with divided identity and the search for a true self.

Dickinson's poem presents marriage as a transformation of identity, comparing girlhood to earthly pain and wifehood to heavenly comfort, but the quotation marks around 'wife' and 'Woman' and the abrupt ending suggest these are social labels. Dickinson, who chose not to marry and devoted herself to poetry, questions whether a woman is complete only in marriage.

Duffy's 'Little Red-Cap' is a feminist revision of a fairy tale and of literary tradition. The girl chooses her experience, learns from the wolf and then rejects him to become an independent poet. Comparing the three: Plath expresses anxiety about the way society sees women's bodies; Dickinson questions marriage; Duffy celebrates female agency. All three use striking imagery and a first-person voice to explore female identity.

Caryl Churchill's Top Girls examines female success within structures shaped by class and gender. Its women come from different historical and social backgrounds, allowing the play to question whether individual achievement alone amounts to liberation.

Mahasweta Devi's Draupadi presents the extreme vulnerability of an Adivasi woman facing state violence. Dopdi's final resistance refuses the shame imposed upon her and transforms vulnerability into defiance.

Top Girls: The dinner scene shows that women across history paid high prices for achievement or survival - Nijo's children were taken away, Joan's child was born in public and she was stoned to death, Griselda gave up her children to prove obedience. Marlene too has abandoned her daughter Angie to her sister Joyce in order to pursue her career. Churchill suggests that 'bourgeois feminism' - individual women succeeding within capitalism - does not help working-class women like Joyce and Angie. The final word, Angie's 'Frightening', looks ahead to an uncertain future.

Draupadi: Mahasweta Devi deliberately recalls the Mahabharata, where Draupadi is disrobed in the Kaurava court but saved by Krishna, who makes her sari endless. Dopdi has no divine protection; her body is violated by the state. Her refusal to be clothed shames the officers and turns the language of honour and shame against them. Spivak reads the story as an example of the subaltern woman's resistance, which breaks the patriarchal and state structures that try to define her.

Comparison: both texts show women in relation to power - Marlene seeks power within the system, Dopdi resists the system - and both expose how class and caste or tribe divide women. Marlene's success is cold and isolating; Dopdi's defiance is powerful even in total defeat.

Alice Walker's The Color Purple traces Celie's development from oppression and silence toward greater independence. Letters give her a means of expression while relationships with other women become important sources of strength.

The novel examines gender violence, racism, family, sexuality, sisterhood and self-respect. Celie's growing ability to speak, work and define herself makes empowerment a central theme.

Narrative form: the epistolary form gives Celie a voice when she has no one to talk to. Her early letters to God are written in plain, ungrammatical black vernacular, showing her lack of education and confidence. As she grows, her language becomes more assured. When she learns that God, as imagined by her, is 'just like all the other mens I know', she stops writing to God and writes to Nettie, and Shug teaches her that God is in everything, including the colour purple in a field.

Themes: (1) gender violence and patriarchy within the black community (Alphonso, Mister, Harpo's attempts to beat Sofia); (2) racism (Sofia's imprisonment for insulting the mayor's wife); (3) female bonding and sisterhood - Celie, Shug, Sofia, Squeak and Nettie support each other; (4) sexuality, including Celie's relationship with Shug; (5) economic independence through the trouser business; (6) African heritage, through Nettie's letters about the Olinka, which show both patriarchy and colonial exploitation in Africa; and (7) forgiveness and change - even Mister becomes a better man.

Walker called her perspective 'womanist' - a black feminism that values women's culture and community. The novel ends with a family reunion on the Fourth of July, with Celie saying she has never felt so young. The colour purple symbolises the beauty and joy of life that God wants people to notice.

The course studies literature from Commonwealth countries and focuses on cultural dilemmas, hegemony, exploitation and the effects of colonisation. Unit I prescribes Helen Tiffin's Commonwealth Literature: Comparison and Judgement.

Commonwealth literature refers to writing in English from countries formerly ruled by Britain, such as India, Nigeria, Kenya, the Caribbean, Australia, New Zealand and Canada. The term was used from the 1960s (the first Commonwealth Literature conference was held at Leeds in 1964). Since the 1980s it has largely been replaced by 'postcolonial literature', a term associated with 'The Empire Writes Back' (1989) by Ashcroft, Griffiths and Helen Tiffin.

Tiffin's essay discusses the difficulty of comparing literatures from very different countries and of judging them by British standards. She argues for comparison based on shared experiences of colonialism - language, displacement, identity and resistance - while respecting each literature's own context.
Colonial rule can alter language, identity, institutions and cultural values. Commonwealth writing often examines how societies respond to these changes and negotiate inherited colonial structures.

Colonised peoples often experience a divided cultural identity: they may be educated in English and Western values while living in societies with their own languages, religions and customs. Frantz Fanon described the psychological damage of colonisation; Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o in 'Decolonising the Mind' (1986) argued that the colonial language colonises thought, and he stopped writing in English for Gikuyu.

Hegemony (Gramsci) means control through consent rather than force: colonial rule made its culture seem superior and natural. Postcolonial writers respond in different ways: rejecting colonial culture, recovering pre-colonial traditions, writing back to canonical texts or celebrating hybridity (Homi Bhabha's term). Settler colonies such as Australia and New Zealand face a different dilemma: building a new identity separate from Britain while confronting the dispossession of indigenous peoples.

sections.title: A Far Cry from Africa – Derek Walcott

blocks.text: Walcott's poem confronts colonial violence in Kenya while expressing the speaker's divided cultural loyalties. It explores violence, colonial history and the conflict of belonging to more than one cultural inheritance.

Derek Walcott (1930-2017), from St Lucia in the Caribbean, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1992. 'A Far Cry from Africa' (1962) responds to the Mau Mau uprising in Kenya (1952-1960), when the Kikuyu fought British colonial rule and both sides committed brutal violence. It opens: 'A wind is ruffling the tawny pelt / Of Africa. Kikuyu, quick as flies, / Batten upon the bloodstreams of the veldt.'

The speaker condemns both the colonial justification of violence and the brutality of the rebels, and compares human violence to nature, where animals kill but do not pretend to fight for a cause. He is of mixed African and European ancestry and educated in English: 'I who am poisoned with the blood of both, / Where shall I turn, divided to the vein?' He loves the English language but cannot accept British violence: 'How choose / Between this Africa and the English tongue I love? / Betray them both, or give back what they give? / How can I face such slaughter and be cool? / How can I turn from Africa and live?' The poem expresses the cultural dilemma of the colonial subject.
The Australian poem explores pregnancy and the intimate connection between woman and unborn child. It presents creation, bodily experience and maternal consciousness.

Judith Wright (1915-2000) was one of Australia's leading poets and an activist for the environment and Aboriginal land rights. 'Man to Woman' is a companion poem to her famous 'Woman to Man', both from 'Woman to Man' (1949), poems about love, conception and pregnancy written when she was expecting her daughter.

When studying the poem, notice how it speaks of the shared creation of a child, the body as the place where life begins and the deep link between love, desire and creation. Wright's imagery draws on nature and the cycles of birth, growth and death. The poem is included in a Commonwealth course to show that Australian writing is not only about colonial questions: personal, bodily and universal experiences are also important subjects. Confirm specific lines from the prescribed text.
Curnow's poem examines questions of settlement, belonging and identity in New Zealand. It reflects tension between inherited European culture and the reality of life in another land.

Allen Curnow (1911-2001) was a leading New Zealand poet concerned with the national identity of settlers. 'House and Land' (1941) shows an old woman, Miss Wilson, the last of an established settler family, living in the decaying house her grandfather built. She is proud of her family and tells the cowman about the old days and about England, which she calls 'home'. Her dog and the cowman, and a visiting historian, appear in the poem.

The historian's comment, 'The spirit of exile ... is strong in the people still', is the key idea: settlers in New Zealand still felt like exiles from England and had not developed a sense of belonging to the land. The cowman, a worker, is more interested in his wages and the pictures (cinema). The poem ends with the 'great gloom' of the land and a lonely, decaying atmosphere. Curnow suggests that New Zealand settler culture had not yet found its own identity, caught between memories of England and an unfamiliar land.

sections.title: I Will Marry When I Want – Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o

blocks.text: The Kenyan play presents exploitation, class inequality and the continuing influence of colonial and capitalist power. The experiences of ordinary workers and peasants expose economic and social injustice.

'Ngaahika Ndeenda' (I Will Marry When I Want) was written by Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o and Ngũgĩ wa Mĩriĩ in Gikuyu and performed in 1977 by villagers at the Kamĩrĩĩthũ Community Educational and Cultural Centre near Limuru. The government banned it, and Ngũgĩ was detained without trial for a year; afterwards he went into exile. This experience led him to write in African languages.

Kĩgũũnda, a poor farm labourer and former Mau Mau fighter, and his wife Wangeci live on one and a half acres. The wealthy Christian businessman Kĩoi and his wife Jezebel, allied with foreign investors, pressure them to have a church wedding and to take a loan on their land title deed. Kĩoi's son John Muhũũni seduces their daughter Gathoni, who becomes pregnant and is abandoned. Kĩgũũnda loses his land. The play criticises the Kenyan elite, religion used to serve power and neo-colonial capitalism. It ends with a song calling the workers and peasants to unite.

Achebe's novel centres on Okonkwo and an Igbo community facing the arrival of British colonial rule and Christian missionaries. It explores tradition, masculinity, social change, cultural conflict and colonial disruption.

Chinua Achebe (1930-2013) published 'Things Fall Apart' in 1958, two years before Nigerian independence. The title comes from W. B. Yeats's 'The Second Coming': 'Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold'. Okonkwo, a famous wrestler and warrior of Umuofia, has built his status through hard work, in reaction against his gentle, debt-ridden father Unoka. His fear of appearing weak makes him harsh; he kills Ikemefuna, a boy who calls him father, because he does not want to look weak.

After he accidentally kills a clansman at a funeral, he is exiled for seven years to his mother's village, Mbanta. During his exile, Christian missionaries arrive, and his son Nwoye converts. When he returns, colonial government and church have divided Umuofia. After the Christian convert Enoch unmasks an egwugwu (ancestral spirit), conflict escalates. Okonkwo kills a court messenger and, when the clan does not rise with him, hangs himself. The District Commissioner plans to write a paragraph about him in a book called 'The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger'.

The syllabus introduces Commonwealth Literature through Helen Tiffin's discussion of comparison and judgement. The course does not claim that individual texts represent entire countries; instead, it uses selected works to explore hegemony, exploitation and cultural dilemmas associated with colonisation.

Students should therefore read the texts in their specific settings while also considering larger questions of colonial power, identity, language and adaptation.

Postcolonial theory provides useful concepts. Edward Said's 'Orientalism' (1978) showed how colonial discourse constructs the colonised as inferior Others. Homi Bhabha discussed hybridity and mimicry - the colonised imitating the coloniser in a way that both copies and subverts. Gayatri Spivak asked whether the subaltern can speak. 'The Empire Writes Back' described how postcolonial literatures 'abrogate' (reject) and 'appropriate' (adapt) the English language to express local experience.

Types of colonial experience differ: invaded or exploited colonies (India, Nigeria, Kenya) where a small British ruling class governed a large indigenous population; settler colonies (Australia, New Zealand, Canada) where European settlers became the majority and the indigenous peoples were displaced; and plantation societies (the Caribbean) created by slavery and indentured labour. The prescribed texts represent all three types.

Common themes include the clash between traditional and colonial cultures, the language question (writing in English or in native languages), identity, exile and belonging, the continuation of exploitation after independence (neo-colonialism) and resistance. Tiffin's caution against judging these works by British standards means students should read each text in its own context and on its own terms.

Derek Walcott's A Far Cry from Africa presents colonial violence and a divided sense of cultural belonging. Judith Wright's Man to Woman turns to the intimate experience of pregnancy and creation. Allen Curnow's House and Land examines settlement and belonging in New Zealand.

These poems demonstrate the range of Commonwealth writing: political conflict, personal bodily experience and cultural identity can all become central literary concerns.

Walcott represents the Caribbean, whose population descends from enslaved Africans, indentured Indians and European colonisers. His poem expresses the hybrid identity of the colonial subject: he condemns colonial violence but loves the English language and culture. The final questions are left unanswered, showing a dilemma that cannot be easily resolved.

Wright (Australia) turns to the private experience of love and pregnancy. Her poems are celebrated for their frankness about the female body and their link of human creation with natural forces. Her inclusion shows that settler-colony writers also sought a distinctive voice; Wright later wrote poems about Aboriginal dispossession and the destruction of the Australian landscape.

Curnow (New Zealand) examines settler identity: Miss Wilson treats England as home while living in New Zealand, and her decaying house represents a colonial culture that has not taken root. Comparison: all three poets deal with belonging. Walcott is torn between two inheritances, Curnow shows settlers who belong to neither, and Wright finds belonging in the body and nature. Their formal styles - Walcott's rhetorical questions, Wright's lyrical intensity, Curnow's ironic narrative - show the range of Commonwealth poetry.

sections.title: I Will Marry When I Want

blocks.text:
Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's I Will Marry When I Want examines Kenyan society through class conflict and exploitation. The play focuses on ordinary people whose lives remain shaped by unequal economic structures even after formal colonial rule.

It criticises the alliance of wealth, power and institutions that benefits elites while workers and peasants struggle. The drama therefore connects colonial history with continuing social and economic inequality.

Context: after independence in 1963, a Kenyan elite (many of whom had collaborated with the British) took over land and wealth, while former Mau Mau fighters and peasants remained poor. Ngũgĩ calls this neo-colonialism: foreign capital and the new African bourgeoisie together continue the exploitation. The play was performed by villagers in their own language in an open-air theatre they built themselves, which made it a political act.

Characters and conflict: Kĩgũũnda and Wangeci represent the exploited peasantry; Gĩcaamba, a factory worker, is the play's political voice, explaining how workers and peasants are exploited. Kĩoi and Jezebel represent the comprador bourgeoisie, using Christianity and modern institutions such as banks to gain more wealth. The Christian wedding and loan are traps, and Gathoni's seduction and abandonment show how the rich exploit the poor even in their families. Kĩgũũnda's loss of his land title deed is the climax.

Techniques: songs, dances and Gikuyu oral traditions are central, and memories of the Mau Mau struggle appear in songs and flashbacks. The play uses satire (the hypocrisy of the Kĩois) and ends with a call for a united struggle by workers and peasants. Themes: class exploitation, land, religion as a tool of oppression, the betrayal of independence and the power of community theatre.

Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart portrays Igbo life before and during the arrival of British colonial rule. Okonkwo is a respected but deeply rigid man whose personal fears and ideals of masculinity shape his actions.

The coming of missionaries and colonial administration creates divisions within the community and challenges established institutions. The novel explores tradition, change, masculinity, religion and colonial disruption while presenting African society with complexity rather than through colonial stereotypes.

Structure: Part One (thirteen chapters) presents Igbo society in Umuofia in detail - its religion, festivals (the New Yam Festival), justice (the egwugwu court), marriage customs, proverbs ('proverbs are the palm-oil with which words are eaten'), farming and family life - as well as Okonkwo's rise and his killing of Ikemefuna. Part Two covers his exile in Mbanta and the coming of the missionaries. Part Three shows his return, the conflict with colonial rule and his suicide.

Okonkwo is a tragic hero: a great man with a flaw - fear of weakness and failure - which makes him rigid and violent. He cannot adapt to change, so he is destroyed by it. Achebe also shows that Igbo society had its own internal problems: the abandonment of twins, the treatment of outcasts (osu) and Okonkwo's harshness drive people like Nwoye towards Christianity. Mr Brown, a tolerant missionary, contrasts with the zealous Mr Smith.

Achebe's purpose: he wrote partly in response to colonial novels such as Joseph Conrad's 'Heart of Darkness' and Joyce Cary's 'Mister Johnson', which presented Africans as primitive. He shows a complex civilisation with its own values, laws and art. The ironic ending, in which the District Commissioner reduces Okonkwo's story to a paragraph, shows how colonial history silenced African voices. Achebe uses English enriched with Igbo words, proverbs and folktales to 'write back' to the empire.
